vulnerabilities.title: STACK_BUFFER_OVERFLOW_ECHO_READ

root_cause.description: The echo function (0x1673) calls read(0, output_buf, 0x1000) reading up to 4096 bytes from stdin directly into the caller's stack buffer (output_buf at rbp-0x110 in child_command_handler). This buffer has only 0x108 (264) bytes of space before the stack canary at rbp-0x8. The read size (0x1000) is a hardcoded constant that vastly exceeds the buffer capacity (0x108). There is no bounds check on the amount of data read versus the buffer size. An attacker can supply up to 4096 bytes of input via stdin, overflowing the 264-byte buffer by up to 3832 bytes, overwriting the canary, saved rbp, return address, and stack frames beyond.

affected_objects: output_buf at rbp-0x110 in child_command_handler frame (264 bytes to canary)

attack_surface.input: stdin (fd 0) - attacker sends 'echo' command via parent, then child reads up to 0x1000 bytes directly from stdin
attack_surface.entry_function: child_command_handler (0x1707) dispatches to echo (0x1673) when strncmp(cmd_buf, 'echo', 4) == 0
data_flow: Attacker sends 'echo' command string to parent via stdin
Parent reads 0x64 bytes from stdin into cmd_buf, writes to pipe1
Child reads command from pipe1 into cmd_buf (rbp-0x180)
echo() called at 0x1876 with rdi = rbp-0x110 (output_buf pointer)
echo() executes read(0, rdi, 0x1000) at 0x1694 - reads up to 4096 bytes from stdin
Attacker-controlled data fills output_buf (264 bytes) then overflows into canary, saved rbp, return address, and beyond
After echo returns, strlen(output_buf) at 0x1896 computes sent_bytes from overflowed buffer
Child writes sent_bytes (4 bytes) and output_buf content to pipe2 for parent

security_check.expected: The read size should be bounded by the actual buffer capacity (0x108 bytes), or the buffer should be large enough to hold 0x1000 bytes, or a length check should prevent reading more than 0x108 bytes.
security_check.actual: read(0, output_buf, 0x1000) with no bounds check. The hardcoded read size 0x1000 (4096) exceeds the buffer capacity 0x108 (264) by 3832 bytes.
security_check.missing_or_incorrect: No bounds check between read size and buffer capacity. The read size is a compile-time constant (0x1000) that does not account for the actual stack buffer size (0x108).

vulnerable_operation.operation: READ into stack buffer with oversized length
vulnerable_operation.expression: read(0, rdi, 0x1000) where rdi = caller's rbp-0x110 (output_buf, 264 bytes to canary)

impact.reason: Attacker-controlled input (up to 4096 bytes from stdin) overflows the 264-byte output_buf stack buffer, corrupting the stack canary, saved frame pointer, return address, and potentially additional stack frames. The overflow is 3832 bytes past the buffer boundary.

Stack canary at rbp-0x8 is overwritten by the overflow. When child_command_handler returns, the canary check at 0x18e3 (cmp rdx, fs:0x28) fails, calling __stack_chk_fail, terminating the child process. If the overflow does not preserve the canary value, the child crashes.

The overflowed output_buf content is passed to strlen() and then written to pipe2 for the parent process. If the overflow fills output_buf with non-null bytes beyond the 264-byte boundary, strlen returns a value larger than 264, causing the child to write overflowed stack data (including canary, rbp, return address values) to the pipe, which the parent then reads. This leaks child stack data to the parent and enables BUG-002.

evidence.description: At 0x1687: mov edx, 0x1000 (sets read size to 4096). At 0x168c: mov rsi, rax (buffer = rdi parameter = caller's output_buf). At 0x168f: mov edi, 0x0 (fd=stdin). At 0x1694: call read@plt. The read size 0x1000 is hardcoded and exceeds the caller's buffer capacity.

At 0x1873: lea rax, [rbp-0x110] (output_buf, 264 bytes to canary at rbp-0x8). At 0x1876: call 0x1673 (echo). The buffer passed to echo is only 0x108 bytes before the canary, but echo reads 0x1000 bytes into it.

Frame size 0x190 (sub rsp, 0x190). Canary stored at rbp-0x8 (mov rax, fs:0x28; mov [rbp-0x8], rax). output_buf at rbp-0x110 has 0x110-0x8 = 0x108 = 264 bytes before canary. echo reads 0x1000 = 4096 bytes, overflowing by 4096-264 = 3832 bytes.

After echo returns: strlen(output_buf) at 0x1896 stores result in rbp-0x188 (sent_bytes). write(pipe2_fds[1], &sent_bytes, 4) at 0x18b8. Then movsxd rdx, eax (sign-extend sent_bytes) and write(pipe2_fds[1], output_buf, sent_bytes) at 0x18d8. If overflow filled buffer with non-nulls, strlen returns large value, and overflowed stack data is sent to parent via pipe.

The overflow corrupts the canary at rbp-0x8. The canary check at 0x18e3 (mov rdx, [rbp-0x8]; sub rdx, fs:0x28; je 0x18f7; call __stack_chk_fail) will detect corruption unless the attacker knows the canary value. However, the overflow also enables data exfiltration via pipe2 (strlen + write of overflowed content), which is a separate impact from the canary-protected crash.

verification_required: Confirm that the child canary can be bypassed or leaked to achieve RIP control in the child process (child is under seccomp, limiting post-exploitation)
Confirm the exact value of strlen(output_buf) after overflow with non-null payload to determine how many bytes are sent to parent via pipe2
Determine if the child's seccomp sandbox (allowing mmap/mprotect) permits useful post-overflow execution despite canary protection

vulnerabilities.title: STACK_BUFFER_OVERFLOW_PARENT_UNVALIDATED_SENT_BYTES

root_cause.description: The parent process (main at 0x1935) reads a 4-byte integer 'sent_bytes' from pipe2 (written by the child process) and uses it directly as the size parameter for read(pipe2_fds[0], output_buf, sent_bytes) at 0x1ade. The output_buf is at rbp-0x110 (264 bytes to canary). There is no validation that sent_bytes is within the buffer capacity (0x108 bytes). The sent_bytes value is sign-extended via movsxd at 0x1ac9, so a negative 32-bit value becomes a very large 64-bit size. The child process computes sent_bytes as strlen(output_buf) after the echo overflow (BUG-001), so if the child's output_buf is filled with non-null bytes beyond its 264-byte boundary, strlen returns a large value that is forwarded to the parent. The parent trusts this cross-process value without any bounds check, causing a stack buffer overflow in the parent process. The parent is NOT under seccomp, so this overflow occurs in an unsandboxed context.

affected_objects: output_buf at rbp-0x110 in main frame (264 bytes to canary)
sent_bytes at rbp-0x188 in main frame (4-byte int from pipe2)

attack_surface.input: sent_bytes (4-byte int) received from child process via pipe2, originally computed as strlen(output_buf) in child after echo overflow
attack_surface.entry_function: main (parent, 0x1935) - reads sent_bytes from pipe2 at 0x1a93, uses it as read size at 0x1ade
data_flow: Attacker sends 'echo' command to parent, parent forwards to child via pipe1
Child's echo reads up to 4096 bytes from stdin into 264-byte output_buf (BUG-001 overflow)
Child computes strlen(output_buf) = sent_bytes. If overflow payload has no null bytes in first N bytes, strlen returns N > 264
Child writes sent_bytes (4 bytes) to pipe2 at 0x18b8
Child writes output_buf content (sent_bytes bytes) to pipe2 at 0x18d8
Parent reads 4-byte sent_bytes from pipe2 at 0x1a93 into rbp-0x188
Parent sign-extends sent_bytes via movsxd at 0x1ac9 (negative int -> huge unsigned size)
Parent calls read(pipe2_fds[0], output_buf, sent_bytes) at 0x1ade with output_buf = rbp-0x110 (264 bytes)
If sent_bytes > 264, parent's output_buf overflows, corrupting canary, saved rbp, return address
Parent is NOT under seccomp - can execute arbitrary syscalls including execve

security_check.expected: The parent should validate that sent_bytes does not exceed the output_buf capacity (0x108 bytes) before using it as a read size. A bounds check such as 'if (sent_bytes > 0x108) sent_bytes = 0x108;' or 'if (sent_bytes < 0 || sent_bytes > sizeof(output_buf)) abort();' should be present.
security_check.actual: No bounds check on sent_bytes. The value read from pipe2 is used directly as the read size after sign-extension via movsxd. There is no comparison against the buffer size or any upper/lower bound.
security_check.missing_or_incorrect: Missing input validation on cross-process trust boundary. The parent trusts the child's sent_bytes value without verifying it is within the buffer capacity. The movsxd sign-extension at 0x1ac9 also means negative sent_bytes values (bit 31 set) become very large 64-bit sizes, though read() would return whatever data is available in the pipe.

vulnerable_operation.operation: READ into stack buffer with unvalidated cross-process size
vulnerable_operation.expression: read(pipe2_fds[0], rbp-0x110, movsxd(sent_bytes)) where sent_bytes is 4-byte int from child via pipe2, output_buf is 264 bytes to canary
vulnerable_operation.size: sent_bytes (attacker-controlled via child echo overflow, up to 0x7fffffff when sign-extended)

impact.reason: The parent reads sent_bytes bytes from pipe2 into a 264-byte stack buffer. If sent_bytes > 264 (which occurs when the child's echo overflow fills output_buf with non-null bytes), the parent's stack is corrupted including canary, saved rbp, and return address. The parent process is NOT under seccomp, so this overflow occurs in an unsandboxed context with full syscall access.
If the overflow corrupts the parent's stack canary at rbp-0x8, the canary check at 0x1b8b (sub rdx, fs:0x28; je 0x1b9f; call __stack_chk_fail) triggers, crashing the parent process.

The parent writes the received data to stdout via write(1, output_buf, sent_bytes) at 0x1afb. If sent_bytes is large and the read succeeds partially, the parent may write stack data (including canary, return addresses) to stdout, potentially leaking sensitive stack contents.

evidence.description: At 0x1a93: call read@plt with edi=pipe2_fds[0], rsi=&(rbp-0x188), edx=4. Parent reads 4-byte sent_bytes from pipe2 into rbp-0x188. This value originates from the child's strlen(output_buf) after echo overflow.

At 0x1ac3: mov eax, [rbp-0x188] (load sent_bytes). At 0x1ac9: movsxd rdx, eax (sign-extend 32-bit int to 64-bit). At 0x1ad2: lea rcx, [rbp-0x110] (output_buf, 264 bytes to canary). At 0x1ade: call read@plt with edi=pipe2_fds[0], rsi=output_buf, rdx=sent_bytes. No bounds check on sent_bytes before this read.

Frame size 0x190 (sub rsp, 0x190). Canary at rbp-0x8 (mov rax, fs:0x28; mov [rbp-0x8], rax). output_buf at rbp-0x110 has 0x108 = 264 bytes before canary. sent_bytes at rbp-0x188 is read from pipe2 without validation.

The child writes sent_bytes = strlen(output_buf) to pipe2 at 0x18b8. After echo overflow (BUG-001), if the attacker fills output_buf with non-null bytes beyond 264 bytes, strlen returns a value > 264. This value is forwarded to the parent, which uses it as read size for a 264-byte buffer. The parent has no seccomp (F007), so this overflow occurs in an unsandboxed context.

The movsxd at 0x1ac9 sign-extends the 32-bit sent_bytes to 64-bit rdx. If sent_bytes has bit 31 set (negative as signed int), rdx becomes 0xffffffff????????, a very large value. read() with this size would attempt to read a huge amount, but the actual data available in pipe2 is limited to what the child wrote. The overflow still occurs if the child wrote more than 264 bytes.

verification_required: Confirm the exact sent_bytes value the parent receives after a specific echo overflow payload (depends on null byte placement in overflowed buffer)
Determine if the parent's stack canary can be leaked or bypassed to achieve control beyond crash
Confirm that the child writes enough data to pipe2 to actually overflow the parent's buffer (child writes sent_bytes bytes of output_buf content, which includes overflowed stack data)
Verify whether the parent's canary check at 0x1b8b can be bypassed (e.g., via canary leak from child's pipe output that includes child's canary value)

non_vulnerabilities.description: prctl(PR_SET_NO_NEW_PRIVS, 1) and prctl(PR_SET_SECCOMP, SECCOMP_MODE_FILTER, &sock_fprog) with return value checks (test eax, eax; jns). BPF filter checks arch == AUDIT_ARCH_X86_64, blocks syscalls >= 0x40000000, whitelists read/write/exit/getuid/getcwd/mmap/mprotect/clock_nanosleep, default KILL.
non_vulnerabilities.reason: Seccomp setup is correctly implemented with proper return value checking. The BPF filter is properly structured with arch check, upper bound check, whitelist, and default-deny. This is a mitigation, not a vulnerability. Note: seccomp only applies to the child process, not the parent.

non_vulnerabilities.function: pipe() and fork() calls in main (0x1967, 0x197b, 0x199e)
non_vulnerabilities.description: pipe() return values checked (cmp eax, 0xffffffff; je error). fork() return value checked (cmp [rbp-0x18c], 0xffffffff; jne continue). Error paths call perror + exit(1).
non_vulnerabilities.reason: Proper error handling on pipe and fork failures. No vulnerability in these system call usage patterns.

non_vulnerabilities.description: Both use strcpy to copy fixed-length strings ('Welcome to the Black C2!\n' = 25 bytes, 'Child Exiting...\n' = 16 bytes) into output_buf (264 bytes).
non_vulnerabilities.reason: The source strings are compile-time constants with known lengths (25 and 16 bytes), well within the 264-byte output_buf capacity. No overflow possible from these functions.

non_vulnerabilities.description: Uses sprintf(output_buf, 'User ID: %d\n', getuid()) to format the UID. Maximum output is 'User ID: ' (9) + max int (10 digits) + '\n' (1) + null (1) = 21 bytes.
non_vulnerabilities.reason: The formatted output is bounded by the maximum integer representation (21 bytes), well within the 264-byte buffer. No overflow possible.

non_vulnerabilities.description: Uses getcwd(cwd_buf, 0x100) into a 256-byte local buffer, then sprintf(output_buf, 'Current working directory: %s\n', cwd_buf). The cwd path is limited to 256 bytes by getcwd, and the formatted string is at most 256 + 26 = 282 bytes.
non_vulnerabilities.reason: getcwd is called with size 0x100 (256) into a 256-byte local buffer (rbp-0x110, frame 0x120). The sprintf output could theoretically be up to ~282 bytes into output_buf (264 bytes to canary), which is a potential minor overflow. However, PATH_MAX is typically 4096 and getcwd with 256 buffer would fail for paths longer than 255 bytes, returning NULL. If getcwd returns NULL, sprintf would dereference NULL, causing a crash but not a controllable overflow. This is a low-severity edge case, not a primary attack surface.

non_vulnerabilities.function: Command dispatch strncmp comparisons in child_command_handler (0x1787-0x1863) and main (0x1b28)
non_vulnerabilities.description: Commands are matched using strncmp with fixed lengths: 'exit' (4), 'banner' (6), 'getuid' (6), 'pwd' (3), 'echo' (4). This is prefix matching.
non_vulnerabilities.reason: Prefix matching means 'echoXYZ' matches 'echo'. This is a design choice for command parsing, not a security vulnerability. The commands are dispatched correctly based on prefix, and no authentication or authorization is bypassed by this matching strategy.

non_vulnerabilities.description: Binary has no RPATH/RUNPATH, only depends on libc.so.6 resolved from system path /lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/.
non_vulnerabilities.reason: No custom .so dependencies, no RPATH/RUNPATH, standard system library resolution. No library hijacking surface.

unresolved.description: Whether the child's stack canary can be leaked or bypassed to achieve RIP control in the child process
unresolved.reason: The child has a canary check at 0x18e3. The echo overflow corrupts the canary. Without knowing the canary value, the child will crash via __stack_chk_fail. However, the overflowed data (including the canary value from the child's stack) is sent to the parent via pipe2 (strlen + write), which could potentially leak the child's canary to the attacker via the parent's stdout output.
unresolved.required_next_step: Dynamic analysis to determine if the child's canary value is leaked through the pipe to the parent and then to stdout, enabling canary recovery for a second exploitation attempt.

unresolved.description: Whether the parent's stack canary can be bypassed when the parent's stack is overflowed via sent_bytes
unresolved.reason: The parent also has a canary check at 0x1b8b. If the parent overflow (BUG-002) corrupts the canary, __stack_chk_fail is called. The parent writes received data to stdout (write(1, output_buf, sent_bytes) at 0x1afb), which could leak the parent's canary if the read from pipe2 includes canary-adjacent stack data. However, the parent reads into output_buf (rbp-0x110), and the canary is at rbp-0x8, so the overflow must reach 264 bytes to hit the canary.
unresolved.required_next_step: Dynamic analysis to determine if the parent's canary can be leaked via stdout output, or if the overflow can be structured to avoid the canary region.

unresolved.description: Whether the movsxd sign-extension of sent_bytes in the parent creates an exploitable negative-size condition
unresolved.reason: At 0x1ac9, movsxd rdx, eax sign-extends the 32-bit sent_bytes to 64-bit. If sent_bytes is negative (bit 31 set), rdx becomes a very large value. read() with a huge size would read whatever is available in the pipe (limited by child's write). The actual overflow depends on how many bytes the child wrote to pipe2, not on the sign-extended size. Need to confirm whether a negative sent_bytes causes any additional issues beyond the positive case.
unresolved.required_next_step: Dynamic analysis to test negative sent_bytes values and confirm the actual read behavior with sign-extended sizes.

unresolved.description: Whether the child process can perform useful operations after echo overflow despite seccomp restrictions
unresolved.reason: The child is under seccomp allowing only read/write/exit/getuid/getcwd/mmap/mprotect/clock_nanosleep. Even if RIP control is achieved in the child (via canary bypass), the seccomp filter prevents execve and most other syscalls. However, mmap and mprotect are allowed, which could enable shellcode execution. The child's primary value is as a stepping stone to overflow the parent (BUG-002) via the pipe communication channel.
unresolved.required_next_step: S3/S4 analysis to determine exploit feasibility under seccomp constraints and whether the parent overflow (BUG-002) is the primary exploitation path.
